headline: Two exploited zero-days open an eight-story day
standfirst: Two in-the-wild exploitation stories lead: a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day attributed to a China-nexus espionage group, and a Collabora CODE Server flaw used to backdoor Nextcloud. Three distinct CVEs appear across the eight selected stories; none is present in CISA's KEV catalog — a confirmed catalog miss, which does not establish that exploitation has not occurred.
bodyMarkdown:
## Actively exploited

BeyondTrust Remote Support, formerly Bomgar, was exploited as a zero-day from late August by the group reported as Armory Castle — previously tracked as UNC5221 and Warp Panda — according to [[s21]]. CVE-2026-102764 is scored CVSS 4.0 9.3, Critical, and classified CWE-290: internal components did not adequately validate the origin of the messages they received, which NVD says could, under the right conditions, let an attacker perform file operations on the appliance. The supplied vector is network-reachable with no privileges and no user interaction required. The story text reports exploitation in the wild, while the CVE is a confirmed miss from CISA's KEV catalog.

The second is a command injection in the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud [[s30]]. CVE-2026-110447 is CVSS 4.0 9.2, Critical — an OS command injection in proxy.php, reachable when the CODE server isn't running, for instance just after a restart — and NVD's record describes it as exploited in the wild in September and October. Scope is narrow and worth checking: standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected, only deployments running CODE Server, and the CVSS attack-requirements field is set to Present, so exploitability depends on the appliance being in the vulnerable state.

## Breaches

Burger King Japan disclosed that attackers accessed a server containing 11.18 million customer records [[s10]]. The Administrative Office of the US Courts, meanwhile, says a cyberattack on contractor BAE Systems took down the notice system federal bankruptcy courts use, halting nationwide noticing [[s19]]. The second is the more instructive: a single supplier's compromise mapping straight onto a court function stopping. Neither story supplies an attacker, a vulnerability or a cause.

## Vulnerabilities

PwnEscape, CVE-2026-99999, is a Linux kernel flaw in networking code that lets code inside a guest virtual machine read memory on the host it runs on [[s31]]. NVD describes an ipv4 checksum validation problem in which bad checksum metadata reaching the stack can let skb_checksum_help corrupt the network header. It carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.3, Critical, with a local attack vector, no privileges, no user interaction, changed scope and High impact across confidentiality, integrity and availability. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes and Vercel confirmed it, per the story. Analysis: the boundary crossed — guest to host — matters more than the local vector, which reflects where the attacker must already be executing code. How broadly exploitable the flaw is in other configurations was not supplied.

## Research

Citizen Lab traced infections at Al Jazeera to Candiru spyware — described in the story as an Israeli maker of spyware sold to governments — delivered through ordinary online ads and requiring no click or other action from the user [[s38]]. The hidden code ran the moment an ad loaded, in some cases with the ad rendering out of sight in the background. Analysis: the delivery channel is the notable part, a mainstream ad path rather than a bespoke lure, which makes the targeting harder to spot from the victim's side. Affected devices and platforms are not stated in the excerpt.

## Industry

CISA and the FBI issued a public service announcement warning election and campaign officials about cyber threats during the 2026 US midterms, flagging phishing and smishing to steal credentials and sensitive information or install malware [[s11]]. Elsewhere, Thoma Bravo-owned Proofpoint will acquire Varonis in an all-cash transaction valued at $6.3 billion, with Varonis going private [[s20]]. Analysis: credential theft remains the named electoral risk while email security spends heavily to move deeper into data security.

nvd.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum

If a packet with bad checksum metadata gets into the ipv4 stack,
skb_checksum_help can corrupt the network header and cause a bunch of
mischief.

This was discovered and reported by Paulos, and has been reporoduced
by others independently since.

We really shouldn't allow such packets in, but as a defence
in depth measure, let's also check before we complete the checksum.

A more complete validation at input is forthcoming, but needs more work.

A request submitted with a nonexistent ID returns a distinct error response code from one submitted with a valid, registered ID, allowing an attacker holding a valid access token - but without further authentication or authorization - to distinguish valid ID values from the full 10-digit numeric search space. Combined with the absence of meaningful rate limiting on this endpoint, this discrepancy constitutes an enumeration oracle, enabling an attacker to discover registered devices at scale.
An attacker can use a hard-coded credential to log in to EseeCloud devices.

nvd.description: Malcolm's nginx based reverse proxy contains a URL path normalization inconsistency between its Lua based role-based access control (RBAC) authorization layer and nginx's own request routing logic. An authenticated user can craft a specially formatted request path to bypass role-based restrictions and reach administrative or role gated endpoints they should not have access to. This affects all restricted paths protected by the RBAC authorization layer, including file upload, PHP server, htadmin, and authentication management interfaces.

Malcolm's nginx Lua role-based access control (RBAC) layer decides whether an authenticated user may reach a role-restricted path (e.g. /htadmin, /auth, /admin_login, /arkime/api/esadmin, NetBox, upload endpoints) by pattern-matching the raw, percent-encoded request URI. Nginx itself, however, selects which location block actually serves the request using the percent-decoded, normalized URI. Because the RBAC check never percent-decodes its input, an authenticated low-privilege user can request an admin-only path using percent-encoding (e.g. /%68tadmin.php) and have nginx route it to the restricted location while the Lua RBAC gate evaluating the un-decoded raw string finds no matching restriction and grants access.

Malcolm's upload-processing pipeline (scripts/safe-extract.py) enforces entry-count, nesting-depth, and total-uncompressed-byte limits when extracting container archives (zip/tar/rar/7z via libarchive), but those limits are not applied when the uploaded file is a single-stream compressed format (.gz, .bz2, .xz, .lzma, .lz) that isn't a .tar.*-style archive. Any authenticated user permitted to upload PCAP/log files can upload a small, highly compressible file (e.g. a gzip bomb) that decompresses to an effectively unbounded size on disk, exhausting the shared Docker volume used by OpenSearch, Logstash, Arkime, and Zeek, and disrupting the platform for all users.

Malcolm's front nginx reverse proxy defines a "Dashboards → Arkime shortcut" location using a case-insensitive regex matcher but a case-sensitive rewrite. A request whose path segment is not exact-lowercase (for example /IDDASH2ARK/...) enters the location (the matcher fires) but evades the rewrite (no redirect is issued), so nginx falls through to the location's proxy_pass to the Arkime backend. That location is the one proxied location in the shipped config that does not include the per-location authentication file, so the request reaches Arkime unauthenticated. The same location also forwards a client-supplied X-Forwarded-User header un-overwritten, and Arkime is configured to trust X-Forwarded-User as the authenticated username — so an unauthenticated network caller can reach the Arkime backend while supplying a forged, auto-provisioned identity.

The Malcolm kiosk Flask application exposes a POST /script_call/<script> endpoint with zero authentication and wildcard CORS (CORS(app)). An attacker can force the operator's browser to execute arbitrary management commands via CSRF, including control.py --wipe which permanently deletes all captured network traffic and forensic logs, or control.py --stop which blinds the security monitoring.

The Arkime live capture service (arkime-live) in Malcolm runs with network_mode: host, exposing port 8005 on all network interfaces (viewHost=0.0.0.0). Arkime trusts the X-Forwarded-User header from any IP address (userAuthIps=::,0.0.0.0/0) and auto-creates users with full access. The passwordSecret is hardcoded to the public value "Malcolm". A network-adjacent attacker bypasses nginx entirely by connecting directly to port 8005 with a forged identity header.

Malcolm file-upload component ships the upstream FilePond PHP server (pqina/filepond-server-php) largely unmodified: Dockerfile copies all upstream *.php files and Malcolm only overwrites config.php and submit.php. Upstream index.php exposes a fetch API route that instructs the server to download an arbitrary URL with curl (including FOLLOWLOCATION) and, for HEAD requests, stores the fetched response body in the upload container's transfer directory and returns the transfer ID to the caller, enabling full readback of the fetched content.
